title: JavaScript Foundations: Runtime Reasoning to a Tested Progress Tracker
description: A browser-and-Node compatible beginner course covering JavaScript runtime values, explicit conversion, conditions, iteration, functions, collections, debugging, and a tested progress-tracker capstone.
prerequisites: Ability to create and save a text file

lessons.title: Running JavaScript and Understanding Values
lessons.summary: Learn how a JavaScript engine evaluates statements, how `const` and `let` bind names, and how to inspect values and runtime errors.
objectives: Explain and apply the JavaScript behavior taught in Running JavaScript and Understanding Values
Test behavior using observable output and assertions

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: JavaScript executes statements through an engine in a browser or Node.js. Prefer `const` when a binding will not be reassigned and `let` when reassignment is part of the design; avoid `var` in new beginner code because function scope and hoisting are easy to misread. A variable holds a value with a runtime type. Use `console.log` and `typeof` to inspect evidence. Read an error from its name and first relevant stack frame instead of guessing. `ReferenceError` commonly indicates an unavailable name, while `TypeError` means an operation was not supported by the received value.

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: JavaScript values include strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, `undefined`, bigints, symbols, and objects. Browser form values are normally strings. Convert intentionally with `Number`, `parseInt`, or `parseFloat`, then verify `Number.isNaN` when failure matters. The `+` operator concatenates when either operand becomes a string, so explicit conversion protects arithmetic. Prefer `===` and `!==` because they compare without type coercion. Template literals use backticks and `${expression}` for readable output. `null` is an intentional empty value; `undefined` commonly means no value was supplied or assigned.

lessons.title: Conditions and Boolean Logic
lessons.summary: Write explicit decisions with comparisons, truthiness, logical operators, optional chaining, and tested boundaries.
objectives: Explain and apply the JavaScript behavior taught in Conditions and Boolean Logic
Test behavior using observable output and assertions

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: An `if` statement selects a branch based on a boolean or a value converted to boolean. Empty strings, zero, `NaN`, `null`, `undefined`, and `false` are falsy; strings such as `'false'` are truthy. Use `&&` when both conditions are required, `||` for alternatives, and `!` to negate. The nullish-coalescing operator `??` supplies a default only for `null` or `undefined`, unlike `||`, which also replaces valid values such as zero. Optional chaining `?.` safely stops property access when the receiver is nullish. Always test values immediately below, at, and above a policy boundary.

lessons.title: Loops and Array Iteration
lessons.summary: Use `for...of`, indexed loops, `while`, array methods, accumulators, and clear termination rules.
objectives: Explain and apply the JavaScript behavior taught in Loops and Array Iteration
Test behavior using observable output and assertions

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Use `for...of` to consume array values directly and a classic indexed `for` loop when the index is part of the problem. `for...in` enumerates property keys and is usually the wrong choice for array values. An accumulator is initialized once before a loop and updated once per accepted item. `while` loops suit state-dependent repetition but must make progress on every normal path. Array methods such as `map`, `filter`, and `reduce` create expressive transformations; begin with a loop when it makes state changes easier to inspect. Avoid modifying an array's length while iterating over that same array.

lessons.title: Functions, Parameters, and Scope
lessons.summary: Create focused functions with explicit contracts, return values, defaults, lexical scope, and testable behavior.
objectives: Explain and apply the JavaScript behavior taught in Functions, Parameters, and Scope
Test behavior using observable output and assertions

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Functions should receive dependencies as parameters and return useful values. A function without an explicit return evaluates to `undefined`; logging is not a substitute for returning data. Function declarations are hoisted, while function expressions assigned to `const` are not usable before initialization. JavaScript uses lexical scope: inner code can read bindings from surrounding scopes, but local bindings do not escape. Default parameters apply when an argument is `undefined`. Arrow functions are concise and capture surrounding `this`; use ordinary functions when dynamic method `this` behavior is intended. Avoid hidden mutation of globals because it makes tests order-dependent.

lessons.title: Objects, Collections, and a Progress Tracker
lessons.summary: Apply arrays, objects, Map, Set, destructuring, immutable updates, and modular design in a progress-tracker capstone.
objectives: Explain and apply the JavaScript behavior taught in Objects, Collections, and a Progress Tracker
Test behavior using observable output and assertions

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Arrays represent ordered sequences. Plain objects are effective records with string or symbol property keys. `Map` supports keys of any type and predictable iteration, while `Set` stores unique values. Destructuring extracts named fields and spread syntax can create shallow copies for immutable updates. A shallow copy does not clone nested objects, so update nested state deliberately. Check own properties with `Object.hasOwn` when inherited names must not count. Separate input/output from domain functions so progress calculations can be tested without a browser. Persisted JSON cannot represent functions, Map, Set, `undefined`, or circular references directly.

finalAssessment.title: JavaScript Learning Progress Tracker Capstone
finalAssessment.instructionsMarkdown: Build a JavaScript progress tracker that adds and updates topics without hidden global mutation, validates percentages, lists completed topics, calculates an average, handles invalid input explicitly, and separates domain functions from browser or console input/output. Include a README and at least ten assertions.
deliverables: Output from at least ten assertions
